concepts.title: Innate Immunity
concepts.contentHtml:
The innate immune system is the body's fast, broad first response. Skin barriers, mucus, antimicrobial peptides, complement proteins, and innate immune cells (macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, NK cells) all act within minutes to hours of infection.

Innate cells recognize PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) — broad signatures of microbes (LPS in bacteria, dsRNA in viruses, β-glucan in fungi) — via pattern-recognition receptors like TLRs.

Innate response: phagocytosis, inflammation, fever, antiviral interferons. Effective for many infections; the foundation on which adaptive immunity builds.

concepts.title: Adaptive Immunity
concepts.contentHtml:
The adaptive immune system is slower (days to weeks for first response) but extraordinarily specific and memory-forming. Two arms: B cells make antibodies; T cells recognize and kill infected cells.

Each B and T cell has a unique receptor generated by random rearrangement of gene segments (V(D)J recombination). The repertoire covers ~10¹¹ possible specificities — enough to recognize essentially any antigen.

Antigen-specific cells expand and form long-lived memory cells. Re-encountering the same pathogen triggers a faster, stronger second response — the basis of vaccine immunity.

concepts.title: How They Cooperate
concepts.contentHtml:
Dendritic cells bridge innate and adaptive: they patrol tissues, eat pathogens, and migrate to lymph nodes to present antigens to T cells.

Cytokines from innate cells direct adaptive responses: IL-12 promotes Th1 (anti-intracellular pathogen); IL-4 promotes Th2 (anti-parasite); IL-6 + TGF-β + IL-23 promote Th17 (anti-fungal/extracellular bacteria).

Adaptive immunity feeds back to innate — antibodies enhance phagocytosis (opsonization) and complement activation. The two systems are intertwined in every successful immune response.

concepts.title: Antibody Structure & Classes
concepts.contentHtml:
An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein. The two arms (Fab) bind antigen; the stem (Fc) interacts with effector cells and complement.

Five isotypes serve different roles: IgM (first responder), IgG (most abundant in serum, crosses placenta), IgA (mucosal surfaces), IgE (allergy and parasites), IgD (B-cell receptor function, less understood).

Class switching during an immune response moves a B cell from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE — the antigen-binding part stays; the effector function changes.

concepts.title: Affinity Maturation
concepts.contentHtml:
In germinal centers (specialized lymph node structures), B cells undergo somatic hypermutation — random mutations in their antibody genes. Cells whose mutated antibodies bind antigen better outcompete the others.

Affinities can improve 100-1000× through several rounds of selection. This is why secondary responses produce higher-affinity antibodies than primary ones.

Affinity maturation is essentially Darwinian evolution within an organism — variation, selection, expansion — happening on a timescale of weeks.

concepts.title: Therapeutic Antibodies
concepts.contentHtml:
Monoclonal antibodies have transformed medicine. Trastuzumab (Herceptin, anti-HER2 in breast cancer), pembrolizumab (Keytruda, anti-PD-1 in many cancers), adalimumab (Humira, anti-TNF in autoimmune disease), rituximab (anti-CD20 in lymphoma).

Several of the world's top-selling drugs are antibodies. They are large (~150 kDa), need injection (can't survive the gut), and are expensive — but their specificity and potency justify the cost.

Antibody engineering — humanization, bispecifics, antibody-drug conjugates — keeps expanding what's possible.

concepts.title: T-Cell Receptors and MHC
concepts.contentHtml:
T cells recognize antigens presented on host cell surfaces by MHC molecules (in humans, HLA proteins). MHC class I (on all nucleated cells) presents endogenous peptides to CD8⁺ T cells (cytotoxic). MHC class II (on antigen-presenting cells) presents exogenous peptides to CD4⁺ T cells (helper).

Each T cell has a unique TCR (similar to antibody, generated by V(D)J recombination). The TCR sees a specific peptide-MHC combination — both must match.

concepts.title: Killer T Cells
concepts.contentHtml:
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells kill infected or cancerous cells by releasing perforin and granzymes (which trigger apoptosis) or via Fas/FasL signaling.

Critical for viral defense: most viruses replicate inside cells, hidden from antibodies. Cytotoxic T cells inspect MHC-I peptides on every cell — if the peptide looks 'wrong' (foreign virus or mutated cancer protein), the cell is killed.

This is also why organ transplants are rejected — the recipient's T cells see donor MHC as 'wrong' and attack.

concepts.title: Helper T Cells & Subsets
concepts.contentHtml:
CD4⁺ helper T cells coordinate immune responses via cytokines. Subsets specialize:

• Th1 (IFN-γ, IL-2): activates macrophages, supports cytotoxic responses — key vs intracellular bacteria, viruses.
• Th2 (IL-4, IL-13): supports B-cell IgE class switching, eosinophil activation — anti-parasite (and allergy).
• Th17 (IL-17): defends against extracellular bacteria and fungi at barriers.
• Tregs: suppress immune responses — preventing autoimmunity.

HIV depletes CD4⁺ T cells, eventually crippling all adaptive immunity. CD4 count is the standard measure of HIV disease progression.

concepts.title: Allergy
concepts.contentHtml:
Allergy is misdirected Th2/IgE response to a harmless antigen (pollen, peanut, dust mite). Crosslinking of IgE on mast cells releases histamine and other mediators — runny nose, hives, anaphylaxis.

Anaphylaxis can kill within minutes from airway swelling and circulatory collapse. Epinephrine reverses the bronchoconstriction and vasodilation.

Modern allergen immunotherapy (sublingual or injection) gradually retrains the immune response over years, often inducing tolerance.

concepts.title: Autoimmunity
concepts.contentHtml:
The immune system attacks self-tissue. Multiple sclerosis (myelin), type 1 diabetes (β cells), rheumatoid arthritis (joint synovium), lupus (DNA, ribosomes, many self-antigens).

Causes are mixed: genetic susceptibility (HLA alleles, other risk genes), environmental triggers (infections, gut dysbiosis), and chance. Female:male ratio is ~5:1 for many autoimmune diseases.

Treatments range from steroids (broad immunosuppression) to highly targeted biologics (anti-TNF for RA, anti-IL-17 for psoriasis, anti-CD20 for MS). Regulatory T cell-based therapies are an emerging frontier.

concepts.title: Immunodeficiency
concepts.contentHtml:
Primary immunodeficiencies are genetic (SCID — severe combined immunodeficiency — affects both B and T cells; agammaglobulinemia removes B cells). 'Bubble boy' patients require sterile isolation or stem-cell transplant.

Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired: HIV/AIDS depletes CD4 T cells; cancer chemotherapy destroys lymphocytes; chronic stress and malnutrition suppress immunity.

Restoring immune function is now possible for some primary deficiencies — gene therapy for SCID (X-linked) was an early gene-therapy success in the 2000s.

concepts.title: Checkpoint Inhibitors
concepts.contentHtml:
Tumors evade T cells by exploiting checkpoint molecules like PD-1 and CTLA-4 — natural brakes on T-cell responses. Antibodies that block these checkpoints (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab) release T cells to attack the tumor.

Game-changing for melanoma, lung cancer, and many others. Allison and Honjo shared the 2018 Medicine Nobel for the discovery.

Some patients have dramatic, durable responses. Others develop autoimmune side effects — the same mechanism that unleashes anti-tumor immunity can unleash off-target.

concepts.title: CAR-T Cells
concepts.contentHtml:
CAR-T cell therapy: take a patient's T cells, engineer them to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that targets a tumor antigen, multiply them, infuse them back.

CAR-T against CD19 (a B-cell antigen) has produced remarkable remissions in B-cell leukemias and lymphomas — including in patients who failed everything else.

Side effects (cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity) can be severe. CAR-T against solid tumors is harder. Technical and biological hurdles remain — but the trajectory is steeply upward.

concepts.title: Future of Immunotherapy
concepts.contentHtml:
Personalized cancer vaccines using mRNA technology are in trials — encode a patient's tumor-specific neoantigens, train the immune system to attack the tumor.

Bispecific antibodies (engaging both T cell and tumor) are approved for several cancers. Allogeneic 'off-the-shelf' CAR-T avoids personalized manufacturing. Tregs are being engineered to control autoimmunity.

Immunotherapy is the most exciting cancer-treatment frontier of the 21st century — and is increasingly being applied beyond cancer.
